prompt: What happens to a Kafka record after every consumer group has read it?

options.text: It is deleted immediately
It stays until retention (time or size) or compaction removes it
It moves to a dead-letter topic
It is archived to object storage automatically

explanation: Kafka is a log: reading only advances each group's offset, and records are removed by retention or compaction policies. (a) describes a queue like RabbitMQ or SQS. (c) only happens if client code publishes failed records there. (d) is not default behaviour; tiered storage is an explicit feature you configure.

prompt: What does the consumer do after restarting?
scenario: A Kafka consumer processed offsets 500 to 599 of partition 2 and wrote results to a database. It last committed offset 560, then crashed.

options.text: Resumes at 600; nothing is reprocessed
Resumes at 560 and reprocesses 560 to 599, so writes must be idempotent
Starts again from offset 0
Skips to the newest offset and loses 560 to 599

explanation: The committed offset is where the group resumes, so records processed after the last commit are processed again: at-least-once. (a) would need a commit at 600. (c) only happens if there were no committed offset and auto.offset.reset were earliest. (d) would need auto.offset.reset=latest with no committed offset.

prompt: How do you repair the read model with the least effort?
scenario: A bug deployed at 09:00 made the `search-indexer` consumer group write wrong prices into Elasticsearch from the `product-updates` Kafka topic. It was fixed at 11:00. Retention is 7 days.

options.text: Restore Elasticsearch from last week's backup
Reset the search-indexer group's offsets to the 09:00 timestamp and let the fixed consumer replay
Ask the product service to republish every product
It can't be repaired; the messages were consumed

explanation: The records from 09:00 are still in the log, so resetting offsets to that timestamp replays exactly the affected window through the fixed code. (a) loses a week of correct updates. (c) works but needs another team and republishes everything. (d) applies to queues, not to a log within retention.

prompt: A topic receives 30,000 records a second. One consumer instance handles 1,000 a second. What is the minimum partition count for one group to keep up?

options.text: 1, with 30 consumers

explanation: You need 30 consumers in parallel, and each partition is read by only one consumer in the group, so at least 30 partitions. (a) gives only 3 active consumers. (c) works but is ten times more than needed. (d) fails because 29 of the 30 consumers would sit idle on a single partition.

prompt: A topic exchange has a queue bound with `order.*.created`. Which routing keys reach it? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: order.eu.created
order.us.created
order.eu.de.created
order.created

explanation: `*` matches exactly one word, so the key must be three words: order, any one word, created. (c) has two words in the middle (it would need `#`). (d) has none in the middle.

scenario: Every one of 40 app servers keeps an in-memory cache and must receive every cache-invalidation message. Each server has its own queue.

options.text: Direct exchange with 40 different routing keys
Fanout exchange with all 40 queues bound
One shared queue that all 40 servers consume from
Headers exchange matching on server name

explanation: Fanout copies each message to every bound queue, which is exactly broadcast. (a) would need the producer to publish 40 times. (c) gives competing consumers: each message reaches only one server. (d) also needs per-server publishing or a header that matches all, which is a roundabout fanout.

prompt: What happens to a message in a RabbitMQ quorum queue after a consumer acks it?

options.text: It is removed from the queue
It stays for 7 days for replay
It is delivered to every other consumer of the queue
It moves to the dead-letter exchange

explanation: RabbitMQ queues are delete-on-ack. (b) describes Kafka retention (RabbitMQ streams are a separate type). (c) is wrong: consumers of one queue compete, each message goes to one. (d) only happens on rejection, expiry, overflow or exceeding the delivery limit.

prompt: Why is throughput so low, and what is the fix?
scenario: A team moved ledger updates to an SQS FIFO queue for ordering. They set MessageGroupId to the constant "ledger" for every message. Throughput is a fraction of what 50 consumers should handle, and most consumers receive nothing.

options.text: FIFO queues only allow one consumer; switch to standard
One message group serialises the whole queue; use the account id as the MessageGroupId
Turn off deduplication
Increase the visibility timeout

explanation: SQS FIFO delivers messages within one group in order, one in-flight batch at a time, so a single group allows almost no parallelism. Per-account groups keep each account ordered while groups run in parallel. (a) is wrong: FIFO supports many consumers across groups, and standard would lose ordering. (c) doesn't affect parallelism. (d) makes redelivery slower but doesn't add parallelism.

prompt: What does SQS FIFO deduplication protect against?

options.text: Any duplicate processing by consumers, forever
The same message being sent again (same deduplication id) within 5 minutes
Two different messages with the same body sent a day apart
Messages being received out of order

explanation: FIFO deduplication drops repeated sends with the same MessageDeduplicationId (or content hash) inside a 5-minute window, which covers producer retries. (a) overclaims: a consumer that doesn't delete before the visibility timeout can still get the message again. (c) is outside the window. (d) is ordering, a separate feature based on message groups.

scenario: Five teams (recommendations, fraud, analytics, search, notifications) all need every user-activity event. Analytics wants to reprocess the last 3 days when it changes its model. Volume is 80,000 events a second.

options.text: One SQS standard queue that all five teams consume from
Kafka: one topic, one consumer group per team, retention of at least 3 days
RabbitMQ direct exchange with one classic queue
SQS FIFO with one message group per team

explanation: Many independent readers, replay of recent history and high throughput are exactly what a log is for. (a) makes teams compete for messages, so each sees only some of them, and there's no replay. (c) has the same competing-consumer problem and no replay. (d) misuses message groups (they partition messages, not readers) and FIFO limits are a poor fit for 80,000/s.

prompt: Which requirements point towards RabbitMQ or SQS rather than Kafka? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Per-message retry with a dead-letter queue built into the broker
New consumers must read data from last month
Routing tasks to different workers by message type or pattern
A small team with no capacity to operate a cluster (SQS)

explanation: Built-in per-message retry and dead-lettering, rich routing and zero-operations are strengths of RabbitMQ and SQS. (b) is the opposite: reading old data needs a retained log like Kafka.
